intended_object: The usual "Sturm chain" sign conditions on a finite sequence of polynomials p₀,…,pₘ over an ordered ring: every entry is nonzero, the last entry has no root, and wherever an interior entry p_i (0<i<m) vanishes, its neighbours satisfy p_{i-1}(x)·p_{i+1}(x) < 0. The condition linking the head to its derivative is left out. This is inferred from the docstring and the module documentation, and from how the library uses it: it is the predicate satisfied by a signed remainder sequence once the gcd has been divided out.
explanation:
The three fields match the standard generalized Sturm sequence conditions.

- **Non-vanishing entries:** `nonzero` says no entry of the chain is the zero polynomial.
- **Last entry has no root:** `last` says the last entry has no root in R.
- **Interior zeros:** `alternate` ranges over consecutive triples (cs[i], cs[i+1], cs[i+2]). So it applies exactly at interior positions. At a zero of the middle entry it requires the outer two values to have product < 0, which is the same as being nonzero and of opposite signs.

The condition on the head (that p₀′·p₁ > 0 at roots of p₀) is deliberately not part of the predicate. The library handles it separately: the variation jump at a root is the sign of p₀′·p₁ (`root_jump`, `sum_sign`). This matches the docstring.

Degenerate cases also behave as intended:
- The empty list satisfies the predicate vacuously.
- A one-entry list only needs a nonzero polynomial with no root.
- A two-entry list `[p, q]` only needs q to have no roots, which correctly makes p and q unable to vanish together.

The generality is right. The definition is stated for an arbitrary linearly ordered strict ordered ring, and that is all its content needs. The theorems that need more (real-closed fields) add those assumptions themselves.

Mathlib has `Polynomial.sturmSeq` and `List` sign variations, but no abstract predicate for Sturm chain conditions. So there is no broader counterpart.
